summary: This informational RFC reports experiences moving a few users to an IPv6-only network that reaches IPv4-only parts of the Internet through NAT64. It covers practical issues, roadblocks, and recommendations on where such networks fit.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people lived with only the new kind of internet address for a while. This is what went wrong and right.

subtitle: Real-world lessons from running networks with IPv6 alone.

tldr.problem: IPv6 is the next-generation Internet protocol, but most of the Internet still runs on IPv4 only. To transition, the IETF designed NAT64, which lets IPv6-only networks reach IPv4-only sites. But does it actually work in practice?
tldr.mechanism: Researchers at Ericsson moved volunteers onto IPv6-only networks with a stateful NAT64 device and DNS64 for two years, testing real applications from email to gaming while accessing the IPv4 Internet through translation.
tldr.outcome: IPv6-only networks are technically viable, but many applications and operating systems had bugs or missing IPv6 support. Dual-stack (both protocols) remains the recommended approach for now, though IPv6-only can work for controlled networks and early adopters.

facts.label: Number of permanent users
facts.value: About 5, plus a dozen occasional users

facts.label: Network setups
facts.value: Office and home environments with heterogeneous hardware

today: RFC 6586 remains informational and reflects experiences from 2010-2012. Since then, IPv6 support has improved in operating systems and applications. The recommendations in the RFC—better DNS discovery, improved firewall support, more IPv6-capable applications, and removal of IPv4 literals—remain largely relevant as networks gradually migrate to IPv6-only in the 2020s.

sections.title: The IPv6-Only Experiment
sections.content: RFC 6586 documents experiences from moving a small number of users to an IPv6-only network, where no IPv4 connectivity was available. Instead of direct IPv4 access, users reached the IPv4 Internet through a NAT64 translator and DNS64 service. The experiment involved both office and home environments with heterogeneous hardware running Linux, BSD, Mac OS X and Windows, testing realistic applications like email, web browsing, instant messaging, voice over IP, gaming and file storage. The experience was from 2010, a time when IPv6 support was less mature than today. The authors note that while dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6) had been used for years in their networks, they wanted to test what would happen if IPv4 was completely unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers asked volunteers to disconnect from the old internet address format and only use the new one. They tracked what worked and what broke.

sections.title: Network Setup and DNS Mechanisms
sections.content: The IPv6-only network was deployed as a separate parallel network alongside the existing dual-stack network. A stateful NAT64 device was installed on the edge, with integrated DNS64 functionality. The NAT64 device provided Router Advertisements so hosts could automatically configure IPv6 addresses. Each IPv6-only network required a /64 prefix for host addresses, and an additional /64 prefix for representing IPv4 destinations in the IPv6 network, totaling a /63 of address space. DNS64 is crucial: when an IPv6-only host queries a domain name that has an IPv4 address record (A record) but no IPv6 record (AAAA record), DNS64 synthesizes a fake AAAA record containing the IPv4 address in a special format. The host then communicates with this synthesized address, which is routed to the NAT64 device. The translator converts the IPv6 packet to IPv4, forwards it to the real destination, and translates the reply back to IPv6. This allows IPv6-only hosts to contact any IPv4 destination as long as it has a DNS A record.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator box sat on the edge of the new network. When a program asked for a website's old-style address, the translator made up a new-style address for it, then secretly forwarded traffic to the real website.

sections.title: Operating System and Application Issues
sections.content: Operating systems themselves had issues despite years of IPv6 support. Linux Router Advertisement information was not automatically updated when networks changed; hosts needed a suspend/resume cycle to restore state. The rdnssd daemon for discovering DNS servers did not work reliably and was not installed by default in some distributions. Mac OS X required explicit configuration to not expect IPv4, and switching between IPv4-only and IPv6-only networks required manual changes to network settings. Microsoft Windows 7 had problems discovering DNS servers via well-known IPv6 addresses without manual configuration. Android lacked automatic DNS discovery mechanisms, requiring custom patches. The authors also observed application-level problems. Perl versions before 5.14 had only partial IPv6 support. Skype, a major instant messaging application, did not work on IPv6-only networks. Many games could not connect to online services or even to local network peers on IPv6. Google Talk did not support IPv6 connections. However, some applications worked well: Facebook, Gmail chat, Jabber, web-based games, and web browsing over HTTP and HTTPS all functioned. Email, software updates, media streaming and many chat systems worked without problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Windows, Mac and Linux all had small bugs nobody noticed because hardly anyone tried the new address format alone. Big applications like Skype and many games just did not work.

sections.title: NAT64 Translation and IPv4 Literals
sections.content: After initial bugs and stability issues were resolved, NAT64 operation itself proved relatively problem-free. There were no unexplained DNS failures or lost sessions. The user experience was comparable to using IPv4 through a traditional NAT44 device. However, one problem stood out: IPv4 address literals embedded in HTML or application protocols. When a web page includes a raw IPv4 address like 192.0.2.1 instead of a domain name, DNS64 cannot synthesize an AAAA record for it because the address is not queried through DNS. The page component becomes unreachable. The authors measured this by downloading the top 1,000 and 10,000 websites from the Alexa popularity list. With the top 1,000 sites, 0.2% required IPv4 literals to render completely; with 10,000 sites, this increased to 2%. In practical web browsing, the authors encountered this only a few times. They also tested web access failure rates: IPv4-only access had a 1.9% failure rate, native IPv6 had a 96% failure rate (because most sites lack IPv6), and IPv6-only with NAT64 had a 2.1% failure rate, matching the IPv4 literal occurrence.
sections.plainLanguage: If a website told your browser to go to a raw number like 192.0.2.1 instead of a name, the translator could not help. This happened rarely but sometimes broke things.

sections.title: Conclusions and Future Work
sections.content: The authors conclude that IPv6-only networking is technically viable and that dual-stack remains the recommended model for general-purpose networking at the time. IPv6-only can be employed by early adopters or highly controlled networks such as mobile networks with operator-driven device selection. The RFC identifies five main improvement areas. DNS Discovery mechanisms are inconsistent across operating systems and not enabled by default in many distributions; standardizing RA-based DNS discovery would help. Network managers in operating systems need more testing on IPv6-only networks. Firewalls need to support IPv6 features equally with IPv4. Applications, especially instant messaging, VoIP and games, need to support IPv6 and avoid IPv4 literals; developers should use IP-version-agnostic APIs. Web content should be cleaned of IPv4 literals. The authors also note that more measurement and testing of VoIP, peer-to-peer, tunneling, mobility and VPN protocols would be valuable. In summary, most issues relate to poor testing and incomplete IPv6 support in applications, not to IPv6 or NAT64 themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The new address format works, but programs need to be updated to use it. Operating systems should help users set it up. Websites should stop using raw numbers. Then everyone can switch.
